title: Blessed is Ram Das
hookLine: the minstrels Satta and Balvand praise the Gurus' light passing on (Ramkali ki Var, ang 968)
tomorrow: I never knew what You did

lines: AND TWO MUSICIANS IN THE ROOM.
cards: Open the Guru Granth Sahib and you find the Gurus' hymns, and the words of saints the Gurus gathered. But a few pages come from people who were in the room with the Gurus.
Among them, tradition says, were two musicians of the Guru's court, Satta and Balvand, who played the rabab and sang.
They watched the line of Gurus pass from one to the next, and they wrote about it the way musicians would: in a ballad, a var.

teach.b: Their var sits in Raag Ramkali, on Angs nine sixty-six to nine sixty-eight. It's short, and it tells one story: Guru Nanak's light passing to Guru Angad, then to Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan.
The line everyone remembers comes early, in a stanza about Guru Angad.

teach.h: ONE LIGHT, ONE WAY, A NEW BODY.
teach.b: In paraphrase: the light is the same, the way is the same; the Master has only changed the body. Jot ohaa, jugat saae.
That single phrase holds the Sikh understanding of the ten Gurus: not ten different teachers, but one light passing from lamp to lamp.
Then, on Ang nine sixty-eight, the stanza for the fourth Guru opens: dhan dhan Raam Daas gur.
Blessed, blessed is Guru Ram Das; the One who made you has also adorned you. The same stanza names him as one with those before him: you are Nanak, you are Lehna, you are Amar Das.
Why does it matter? Because the var is a witness.
Not a theologian explaining succession, but two singers close enough to see it, saying: we watched the same light move.
Sikhs still sing their var, and jot ohaa jugat saae is often quoted when people speak of the Gurus as one. And the musicians' own names, Satta and Balvand, are in the Guru Granth Sahib forever.
The people who carried the tune are kept in the book.

how: Sikhs sing Satta and Balvand's var in kirtan, and quote its phrase about the same light and the same way when speaking of the ten Gurus as one.

o: a musician's skill, passed to a student
a lamp lit in the gurdwara at dusk
light, the same flame in every Guru

games.q: the minstrels' var — tap the pairs.
p: court musicians who wrote the var

s: every hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib was written by a Guru
the Gurus also included saints, and musicians like Satta and Balvand.
the var says the light stays the same while the body changes
jot ohaa jugat saae: one light, one way, a new body.

games.q: you're one of the Gurus' musicians, watching the leadership pass to a new Guru. what does the var say you saw?
o: the same light in a new body.
games.why: the light is the same, the way is the same; only the body changed. Sikhs still speak of the Gurus as one light.

practice: Think of a person you admire, and ask who taught them: a parent, a coach, a mentor, a grandmother, a book.
Picture the light passing from that teacher to them, and maybe from them to you, and silently say: blessed is the one who taught them. If you pray, say Waheguru in thanks for that line of teachers.

wordCard.voice: Jot, light: the musicians Satta and Balvand's ballad about the fourth Guru says the jot is the same, the way is the same, and only the body changes.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: light; the var says the jot, the light, passed unchanged from Guru to Guru.

carryVoice: Your line: the light passes on. One flame, many lamps. Six hundred sixty-nine days, and counting.

sources.ref: Ramkali ki Var, Rai Balvand and Satta Doom (jot ohaa jugat saae), Ang 966
